comparison: Both strongly support the core finding that β-carotene promotes atherosclerosis resolution across multiple models (C5, C48). OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from ASO-LDLR and Ldlr-/- models with statistical validation. Peer reviewers affirm robustness through multiple models and solid evidence for T cell contributions. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with high confidence.

Both address the lack of β-carotene effect on plasma lipids during resolution (C28-C30, C41-C42). OpenEval notes this is appropriately documented and distinguished from progression studies. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms the data showing no differences in plasma lipids, validating this finding. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address plaque composition measurements (C35, C44). OpenEval supports consistent findings across models. Peer reviewers accept aortic root measurements without challenge, though note limitations regarding en face preparations not included in these specific claims. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address collagen content findings (C36-C38, C45-C46). OpenEval supports convergent evidence from two models. Peer Reviewer 1 specifically notes collagen content as a robust β-carotene effect and identifies it as the major CD25+ cell dependent effect. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address Bco1-/- genetic evidence (C6, C49-C56). OpenEval strongly supports this as mechanistic evidence that vitamin A production mediates effects. Peer reviewers accept the genetic evidence but Reviewer 2 notes lack of direct Treg data in Bco1-ko mice, indicating the mechanistic link to Tregs specifically needs more support. OpenEval: SUPPORTED, Peer: SUPPORTED with caveats.

Both address Treg expansion in plaques (C7, C66-C67). OpenEval supports the finding with convergent evidence from pharmacological depletion and genetic knockout. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, noting the title claims are not fully measured and cautioning about small sample sizes for FoxP3+GFP+ cell quantification. Significant disagreement: OpenEval SUPPORTED vs Peer UNCERTAIN.

Both address the role of BCO1 in Treg expansion (C142-C143). OpenEval supports this as directly implicating vitamin A formation in Treg effects. Peer Reviewer 2 notes lack of experimental Treg data in Bco1-ko mice to support this mechanistic claim. Disagreement: OpenEval SUPPORTED vs Peer UNCERTAIN.

Both address anti-CD25 depletion effects (C8, C62-C63, C74-C82, C162-C163). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to incomplete depletion and marginal statistical significance. Peer reviewers also express UNCERTAINTY, noting partial suppression, potential confounding by CD25+ effector T cells, and suggesting alternative approaches. Strong agreement on UNCERTAIN evaluation.

Both address discriminant analysis results (C80-C82). OpenEval notes marginal statistical significance (FDR=0.10) contributing to UNCERTAIN evaluation. Peer reviewers accept discriminant analysis without challenge as supporting overall conclusions. Mild disagreement on interpretation strength.

Both address Treg-independent macrophage effects (C86-C88). OpenEval supports these findings as demonstrating effects persist with anti-CD25 treatment. Peer Reviewer 1 acknowledges this addresses concerns about retinoic acid signaling in lesions and confirms other cells besides Tregs are impacted. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address negative findings on monocyte recruitment and proliferation (C89-C90). OpenEval supports these as ruling out alternative explanations. Peer reviewers accept these negative findings without challenge. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address body weight and plasma lipids during resolution (C25-C27, C40, C60, C116). OpenEval supports the consistent finding of no differences and notes appropriate distinction from progression studies. Peer reviewers accept these findings and the attention to potential confounders. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address vitamin A measurements (C32-C33, C43, C50, C146-C147). OpenEval supports HPLC measurements ruling out deficiency and showing increased hepatic vitamin A. Peer reviewers accept these measurements without challenge, with Reviewer 1 noting successful supplementation. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address Cyp26b1 as a retinoic acid signaling marker in lesions (C134-C138). OpenEval supports this as validated marker with translational relevance. Peer reviewers specifically acknowledge this addresses initial concerns about measuring retinoic acid signaling in lesions rather than just liver. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address incomplete Treg depletion limitation (C151-C153). OpenEval supports the transparent acknowledgment of this limitation. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this limitation and note it is known for the anti-CD25 approach. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED regarding the acknowledgment of limitations.

OpenEval rates speculative explanations for discrepancies between resolution and progression studies (C117-C120) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are untested hypotheses. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these mechanistic speculations.

OpenEval rates claims about unknown source of vitamin A for Treg differentiation (C164-C171) as UNCERTAIN, noting multiple possibilities are presented without experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this mechanistic gap.

Peer reviewers accept discriminant analysis results (C39, C47, C55, C80-C82) as supporting overall conclusions about β-carotene effects. OpenEval addresses some of these claims in R1 and R4 but does not have a dedicated evaluation of the discriminant analysis methodology itself.
